language.script_notes: Latin alphabet with å, ä, ö. The ö (not ø) is the quick separator from Norwegian; Danish and Norwegian use ø and æ instead. Street-name suffixes -gatan ('street') and -vägen ('road'); 'Enkelriktat' marks one-way streets. .se domain.

road_furniture.bollard_color: White post with a black band roughly one third from the top; a small white rectangle sits inside the black band. Reflectors can be orange near junctions.
road_furniture.bollard_shape: Flat-faced post (not cylindrical), in a few variants — wedge, rounded, or thin and slightly curved.
road_furniture.guardrail_type: Standard steel W-beam; Sweden also pioneered '2+1' roads with a wire-rope median barrier, which is a strong Sweden/Nordic tell when present.
road_furniture.line_paint: White centre line and white dashed edge lines. The gaps between edge dashes are noticeably longer than the dashes — Norway's dashes are longer, Denmark's shorter. Yellow centre lines point away from Sweden toward Norway.
road_furniture.curb_style: No strongly distinctive curb style noted.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Wooden utility poles are common. Chevron (bend) boards and route-number signs carry the yellow-and-blue national colours; Norway and Finland lean on yellow-on-black instead.

architecture.roof_style: Mostly simple gabled roofs; no single iconic roofline.
architecture.roof_material: Clay tile and profiled sheet metal both common.
architecture.wall_construction: Painted timber panelling is very common in rural and small-town buildings; plaster and brick in cities.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Deep 'Falu red' (Falu rödfärg) is iconic, often with white window trim; also mustard yellow and white.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Falu-red wooden houses and barns throughout the countryside. Larger towns have plastered 18th–19th-century blocks and mid-century apartment estates.

nature.vegetation: Open farmland across the far south (Skåne); a mixed conifer-and-broadleaf belt through the middle; dense spruce/pine taiga in the north with few broadleaf trees.
nature.terrain: Mostly flat to gently rolling, dotted with lakes. Real mountains (the Scandes) appear only along the Norwegian border in the north-west.
nature.climate_signature: Snow is common in winter and lingers far longer in the north. Low sun angle and long shadows for much of the year; a generally cool, muted light.

vehicles.plate_color: White with the blue EU strip and 'S'.
vehicles.plate_format: Three letters, a space, then three characters — historically ABC 123, newer issues ABC 12A. Not geographically coded.
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: A high share of Volvos, but not diagnostic on its own. No strong car-based meta.

google_coverage.blur_style: Standard Google blurring, nothing unusual noted.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: White Google car. When the car is visible it often shows a long roof antenna, and sometimes a white rear panel with a faint blue stripe. Broad rural coverage including snowy conditions.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Falu-red timber houses, Latin script with extra vowels, snowy conifer landscapes, wooden poles
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Sweden uses a WHITE centre line and yellow/blue chevron and route signs; Norway uses a YELLOW centre line. Sweden's ö vs Norway's ø on signage. Norway is far more mountainous with fjords.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Falu-red houses, snow-heavy coverage, similar flat-faced bollards, Nordic road furniture
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Language is the instant tell — Finnish (long words, doubled letters, -tie, Oy) looks nothing like Swedish. Finland is flatter, has far more lakes and gravel roads, and its bollards read as cylindrical rather than flat-faced.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Scandinavian language feel, EU plates, similar signage
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Denmark is uniformly flat farmland with almost no forest or snow, uses shorter edge-line dashes, and has a distinct bollard and plate style. No snow poles.
